title: Crystals & Symmetry
description: How atoms arrange themselves and why it matters

concepts.title: The Crystal Lattice
concepts.contentHtml:
A crystal is a periodic arrangement of atoms that repeats forever in three dimensions. Each unit cell — the smallest repeating block — defines the whole structure.

There are exactly 14 distinct three-dimensional lattices (the Bravais lattices) and 230 crystal symmetry groups. Salt is simple cubic; copper is face-centered cubic; ice is hexagonal.

The lattice constant — typically a few angstroms — sets the scale. X-ray diffraction reads it directly via Bragg's law.

concepts.title: Reciprocal Space & the Brillouin Zone
concepts.contentHtml:
For a periodic crystal, momentum (or wavevector) is most naturally indexed in reciprocal space — a Fourier-dual lattice.

The first Brillouin zone is the unit cell of reciprocal space. Electron and phonon dispersions are typically plotted across this zone.

Symmetry of the lattice carries over to symmetry of the Brillouin zone. Special high-symmetry points (Γ, X, K, M…) appear repeatedly in band-structure diagrams.

concepts.title: Defects
concepts.contentHtml:
Real crystals are imperfect: vacancies, interstitials, dislocations, grain boundaries.

These defects control most material properties we care about — strength, conductivity, color. Pure silicon is an insulator; doped silicon (one phosphorus per million atoms) is a semiconductor that runs the modern world.

Working metals — bending, hammering, forging — moves dislocations. Heat treating annihilates them. The mechanical behavior of metals is, more than anything, defect physics.

title: Electrons in Solids — Band Structure
description: Why some materials conduct, some insulate, some are in between

concepts.title: Energy Bands
concepts.contentHtml:
An isolated atom has discrete electron energy levels. Bring 10²³ atoms together and those levels broaden into bands — continuous ranges of allowed energies separated by forbidden gaps.

This is the consequence of Bloch's theorem: in a periodic potential, electronic states are plane waves modulated by lattice-periodic functions, indexed by a wavevector k in the Brillouin zone.

concepts.title: Metals, Insulators, Semiconductors
concepts.contentHtml:
Filling rules decide everything. If the highest occupied band is partially filled, the material is a metal — electrons can move freely.

If a band is completely full and the next band is far above, you have an insulator. If the gap is small (about 1 eV), it's a semiconductor — thermally accessible carriers, conductivity controllable by doping.

Silicon (gap 1.1 eV), germanium (0.7 eV), gallium arsenide (1.4 eV) — these powered the digital revolution.

concepts.title: Electrons & Holes
concepts.contentHtml:
An empty state in an otherwise-full band behaves like a positive charge carrier — a hole.

This is why semiconductors are versatile: dope with phosphorus (extra electron) to get n-type; dope with boron (one fewer electron, leaving a hole) to get p-type. A p-n junction is the basis of every diode and transistor.

title: Phase Transitions & Magnetism
description: Order from disorder, and where universality comes from

concepts.title: Order Parameters
concepts.contentHtml:
Phase transitions break symmetry. Liquid water has full rotational and translational symmetry; ice has only the discrete symmetries of its crystal lattice.

The order parameter measures the broken symmetry. For a magnet, it's the magnetization M. For a superconductor, the macroscopic wavefunction's amplitude. For a fluid, density variations.

concepts.title: The Curie Temperature
concepts.contentHtml:
A ferromagnet (like iron) has aligned spins below a critical Curie temperature T_C and disordered spins above. Iron's T_C is 1043 K.

Heat a magnet past its Curie point — the magnetization vanishes; the symmetry is restored. Cool back below — spontaneous magnetization picks a direction (this is spontaneous symmetry breaking).

The Ising model — spins on a lattice, neighbors prefer to align — captures this transition. Onsager solved it exactly in 2D in 1944.

concepts.title: Universality & Critical Exponents
concepts.contentHtml:
Near a continuous phase transition, quantities like specific heat and correlation length diverge as power laws. The exponents — α, β, γ, ν — depend not on microscopic details but only on the dimension of space and the symmetry of the order parameter.

This is universality: water near its critical point and a 3D Ising magnet near its Curie point share the same exponents. Different physics, same critical behavior.

The renormalization group (Wilson, Nobel 1982) explains why: only the long-wavelength fluctuations matter near criticality.

title: Superconductivity
description: Zero resistance and the macroscopic quantum

concepts.title: Zero Resistance & the Meissner Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Below a critical temperature T_c, certain materials lose all electrical resistance — current flows forever without dissipation. Mercury, T_c = 4.2 K, was the first (Onnes 1911).

Superconductors also expel magnetic fields entirely (the Meissner effect). They aren't just perfect conductors; they're perfect diamagnets. This is why a magnet floats above a cooled superconductor — a striking demonstration.

concepts.title: BCS Theory & Cooper Pairs
concepts.contentHtml:
BCS theory (Bardeen, Cooper, Schrieffer 1957) explains conventional superconductors. Electrons attract each other indirectly via lattice vibrations — the lattice deforms slightly around one electron, attracting another.

This binds them into Cooper pairs with zero net momentum and spin. Cooper pairs are bosons; macroscopic numbers of them condense into a single coherent quantum state. Resistance vanishes because individual scatterings can't break that condensate.

concepts.title: High-T_c & Open Problems
concepts.contentHtml:
BCS predicted no superconductors above ~30 K. Then in 1986, Bednorz and Müller found copper-oxide superconductors with T_c above 90 K — high enough to use liquid nitrogen rather than liquid helium.

Despite four decades of work, the mechanism in these cuprates is not fully understood. Hydrogen-rich materials under extreme pressure have shown superconductivity above 200 K. Room-temperature ambient-pressure superconductivity remains the holy grail.

concepts.title: The Quantum Hall Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Apply a strong magnetic field to a 2D electron gas at low temperature, and the Hall conductance — current per voltage at right angles — becomes quantized in exact integer multiples of e²/h.

The quantization is robust: it doesn't care about disorder, sample shape, or material details. This is the first hint that some phases of matter are characterized by topology, not local symmetry breaking.

The quantum Hall effect now defines the SI unit of resistance.

concepts.title: Topological Insulators
concepts.contentHtml:
A topological insulator is insulating in its bulk but has metallic states on its surface, protected by topology. You can't get rid of the surface states without closing the gap or breaking the symmetry.

The surface states have spin locked to momentum — useful for spintronics. Predicted in 2007, observed in bismuth-telluride compounds shortly after.

This was a major shift in condensed matter: phases not characterized by an order parameter, but by a topological invariant of the band structure.

concepts.title: Beyond Topology — Strongly Correlated Materials
concepts.contentHtml:
Many of the most interesting modern materials are strongly correlated — electron-electron interactions can't be treated as a small perturbation.

Cuprates, heavy fermions, frustrated magnets, twisted bilayer graphene — these systems show high-T_c superconductivity, exotic magnetic order, fractional charge, and emergent gauge fields.

Condensed matter has become a laboratory for exotic quantum field theory. Many-body localization, fractons, non-Fermi liquids — concepts that started here are being exported to other parts of physics.
